findings.description: The ledger exports bucket, which holds financial ledger data, defines no server_side_encryption_configuration and therefore does not apply customer-managed KMS encryption to stored objects. Data written here relies solely on AWS defaults rather than an explicit encryption policy.

The reports bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration block, so reports (including the uploaded vendor-roster.xlsx) are not encrypted with an explicit KMS key at rest. This is the destination for the seed object and lacks any stated encryption policy.
The model artifacts bucket defines versioning and access logging but no server_side_encryption_configuration, leaving stored model data without customer-managed KMS encryption.
The ops runbooks bucket enables versioning and sets a private ACL but provides no server_side_encryption_configuration, so objects are not encrypted with an explicit KMS key at rest.

No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is defined for the audit bucket, so there is no guardrail preventing a future bucket policy or ACL from making audit logs public; the acl = "log-delivery-write" grants the log delivery group write access and should be constrained by an explicit public-access block.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is defined for the ledger bucket, leaving no explicit control that prevents the bucket or its objects from being made public in the future.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is defined for the reports bucket, so accidental or malicious public exposure of report data is not blocked at the bucket level.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is defined for the model artifacts bucket, leaving no explicit control preventing future public exposure of stored artifacts.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is defined for the ops runbooks bucket, so there is no guardrail enforcing that the bucket remains private.
